||The United States has 121 million ha of marginal land that could be used to produce renewable energy.Approximately 1.73 million ha of this land includes federally funded brownfelds, closed landflls, andabandoned mine lands. This study presents a GIS model to evaluate a range of site-specifc energy pro-duction potentials on brownfelds, closed landflls, and abandoned mine lands. Five energy sources areconsidered: soybeans, sunfowers, and algae for biodiesel, and solar and wind for electricity. Using soybeans,sunfowers, and algae, the United States could produce 39.9103 TJ–59.1103 TJ of renewable fuel per yearfrom biodiesel. Using solar and wind resources, the United States could produce 114–53 TW h per year ofelectricity. The lower end of the range for each resource represents marginal yields as expected undermarginal conditions. The upper end of the range represents prime conditions and is used for comparison toother, more productive types of land and U.S. regional climates. While renewable energy sources sited onindividual sites may produce marginal amounts of energy, strategic uses of land and combinations ofsources can supplement the national energy matrix. ## 1. Introduction

## 1.1. Motivation and background

Recent studies have highlighted irreversible impacts of agriculture as well as direct and indirect land use change related to energy production [1–4]. Regarding biofuels, and ethanol in particular, Searchinger et al. [5] found that inclusion of land use change in the life-cycle emissions from corn-based ethanol (a firstgeneration biofuel) results in a 93% increase in total greenhouse gas emissions (GHGs) in comparison to conventional gasoline [5]. The same calculation for switchgrass-based ethanol (a secondgeneration biofuel) results in a 50% total increase in GHGs compared to gasoline [5]. Microalgal biodiesel (a third-generation biofuel) shows promise for reducing GHGs [6,7]. However, like many biofuels, microalgal biodiesel can also exhibit positive or negative net energy results depending on cultivation and conversion pathways [8].

All biofuel feedstocks require nutrient inputs, water (often via irrigation), and suitable growing conditions [9]. Some feedstocks, however, are more resilient than others and can grow successfully on marginal lands. Peterson and Galbraith [10] first defined marginal land as “land on the margin of cultivation [...] the poorest land that can be remuneratively operated under given price, cost, and other conditions” [10]. Shortall [11] considers three varieties of marginal land to be of particular importance: 1) land unfit for food production, 2) land of ambiguously lower quality, and 3) economically marginal land [11]. Milbrandt et al. [12] describe marginal lands as abandoned, underutilized, and idle [12]. Nearly all definitions refer to poor physical and chemical soil properties and susceptibility to erosion [4,13–15]. Furthermore, there is a lack of knowledge regarding feasible and consistent energy crop yields on different types of marginal lands. This study evaluates brownfields, closed landfills, and abandoned mine lands as a subset of marginal lands available for renewable energy production.

Producing renewable energy on marginal lands, when done strategically and with regard to the entire life cycle, could potentially reduce the amount and intensity of inputs required for energy production. Scientific and legislative interest is growing in this area of land-constrained energy production, whether in the case of biofuel crops that can withstand poor soil quality and help meet energy mandates [11,12,16–19] or in the case of building renewable energy facilities on contaminated sites that would otherwise remain unused [12,20]. The U.S. EPA program: “REPowering America's Land”, for example, encourages development of renewable energy projects on currently and formerly marginal and contaminated lands and provides resources to communities engaging in such projects [20]. Despite growing interest, previous studies have focused on bioenergy and have largely ignored nonagricultural sources, such as solar or wind [21–23].

Some studies claim that using marginal lands to produce bioenergy on a global scale is unfeasible for reasons such as the lack of economic incentives, disturbances to food security, and threats to biodiversity and conservation areas [3,24]. Other studies state that global feasibility estimates vary but marginal production levels become more viable when considered on the regional level [25]. Still others, as in this study, focus on symbiotic relationships between the land, regional characteristics, and the renewable energy potential available [26]. Every geographic and climatic region is different, and therefore spatial analyses are crucial to designing sustainable solutions for land use and for energy infrastructure systems [27]. A variety of energy production technologies can be employed. This study evaluates the energy that can be produced on marginal sites by cultivating soybeans, sunflowers, and algae for biodiesel, and by implementing solar and wind technologies for electricity.

## 2. Methods

One of the primary challenges in assessing the amount of marginal land available in an area is deciding what qualifies as “marginal” for the region being evaluated. While diverse definitions exist [10,14,17,28], marginal land is generally classified as land unfit for food-grade agriculture and not otherwise fulfilling conservational purposes or ecosystem services. This study limits consideration of marginal land to three types of marginal sites: brownfields, closed landfills, and abandoned mine lands (AMLs).

## 2.1. Land data

The 48 contiguous states were mapped in the GIS program ArcGIS 10. Table 1 lists the sources and types of GIS data layers used in the analysis. Each of the three site types—brownfields, landfills, and abandoned mine lands—were imported as XY data and projected using the NAD83 datum. Since no polygon shapefiles were available, the area of each site was determined from existing databases. The AML site area was extracted from the Abandoned Mine Land Inventory System (e-AMLIS) for each mine where the mine's status was listed as complete [29]. The site areas for closed landfills and brownfields were extracted from the EPA's RE-Powering database and matched by site name and location to the mapped points [30]. Fig. 1 depicts the GIS process used to join the site data with the energy source data, resulting in energy production potentials on each site.

After removing sites with areas given as zero or null, 15,808 (of 18,738) brownfields, 588 (of 843) closed landfills, and 25,114 (of 50,483) abandoned mine lands remained. Table 2 summarizes the site areas, including minimum, maximum, mean, and total site areas before considering any energy siting options.

## 2.2. Modeling feedstocks and yields: soybean, sunflower, and algae

Soybean, sunflower, and algae were evaluated as agricultural feedstocks on the brownfields, closed landfills, and AMLs. The GIS model used to calculate the microalgal growth rates on these sites was constructed in ModelBuilder in ArcGIS 10. ModelBuilder allows the user to automate complex GIS processes and describe geoprocessing procedures in a visual manner. To estimate the volumes of soybean and sunflower biodiesel, respectively, the product of four factors was computed: site areas, crop yields from USDA census records, oil content of the seeds, and harvest and conversion efficiencies [31]. Details of these calculations can be found in Appendix A. The lower 20% of USDA yields were used to model sunflower and soybean crop growth on contaminated sites. Low yields for sunflowers were assumed to range from 560 to – 1120 kg/ha (500 1000 lb/acre) while low yields for soybeans were assumed to range from 1010 to 1340 kg/ha (15–20 bu/acre) [32]. No sites were eliminated due to excessive contamination. Different site types will lead to different yields due to soil conditions, e.g. soils on AMLs tend to be contaminated with heavy metals and the soils on brownfields are often acidic [33,34]. Algae yields were computed using ModelBuilder in ArcGIS 10. The rate of solar insolation was multiplied by a product of efficiency factors and divided by the lower heating value to obtain the microalgal growth rate. Details of this calculation can be found in Appendix A. Fig. 2 shows the algae production rates, which are based on levels of solar insolation. This study uses the algae strain Chlorella vulgaris and assumes it is cultivated in flat-plate photobioreactors (PBRs) [35,36]. The PBRs are assumed to occupy 80% of each suitable marginal site to allow space for access and maintenance. The PBR surface-to-volume ratio is 80.1 m[2] /m[3] , where 80–100 m[2] /m[3] is considered optimal [35]. The PBR dimensions are 50 m long by 20 m high by 0.025 m wide. The growth rate was multiplied by the surface area of the PBR to determine the sitespecific biomass production volume, which was converted to biodiesel volume using the density conversion of 870 kg microalgal biodiesel/m[3] biomass, 30% lipid content, and energy content conversion of 41 MJ/kg microalgal biodiesel.

## 2.3. Modeling non-agricultural sources: solar and wind

Solar energy production is a natural extension of microalgal biodiesel production, and vice versa, as both processes require similar climatic conditions for optimal solar insolation. This study uses Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) to measure solar insolation. Measured in kW h/m[2] day, GHI is defined as the sum of the

direct normal irradiance (DNI) projected onto a horizontal surface plus the diffuse horizontal irradiance (DHI) [37]. GHI in the United States ranges from approximately 3.0–5.8 kW h/m[2] day. This study assumes a utility-scale single-axis tracking photovoltaic (PV) system (0° tilt) with a standard efficiency range of 0.15–0.35 [38]. Fig. 2 depicts the national PV potential under these conditions, which could be adjusted based on site-specific needs. Details of the PV power calculation can be found in Appendix A.

Wind power ranges were mapped at the 50-m hub level, as shown in Fig. 3, using state-based GIS layers compiled by NREL [38]. No data is available at the 50-m level for Alabama, Louisiana, Florida, and Mississippi, therefore these states were excluded from the wind analysis. Trends in turbine construction indicate that 80m hub heights are becoming more common. In 2013, the average hub height was 80 m, which represents an increase of 45% since 1999 [39]. Analyses using 50-m hub levels likely result in an underestimate of the production potential since wind resources tend to increase with hub height, however the 50-m levels were retained in this analysis due to lack of geospatial wind data publicly available at the 80-m level.

Wind power was divided into classes according to the Wind Power Class (WPC) system [40]. WPC ratings range from 1 to 7, where WPCr 2 is considered marginal (0–200 W/m[2] ) and 7 is considered superb (800–2000 W/m[2] ). To estimate the national wind power potential, areas in m[2] of brownfields, closed landfills, and AMLs were multiplied by the WPC ratings and a typical capacity factor range of 0.25–0.40 [41,42]. Details of the wind power calculation and the Wind Power Class system can be found in Appendix A.

Both solar and wind technologies have two primary options regarding energy deployment: decentralized or “distributed” generation and grid-connected systems. Each comes with its own advantages and challenges. While electric generation potential is often abundant at the distributed level, solar and wind resources are often located in rural areas and far from high-demand urban centers [39,43]. Depending on the quality and intensity of solar insolation, it may be economically favorable to build transmission lines from rural solar sources to urban power utilities. Alternatively,

new generation facilities may be built closer to urban centers. Distributed PV systems may also be integrated into regional electric grids, especially as smart grids become more widespread. Transmission and distribution of electricity typically results in energy losses around 6% [44]. In addition, developers must prove the exhaustion of distributed options and the necessity of additional transmission lines before any new construction takes place [43]. Given a combination of distributed and grid-connected technologies, wind power capacity could reach 224 GW by 2030, up from 61 GW in 2013 [39]. Similarly, solar PV installations could total 302 GW by 2030, which would require a national installation rate of approximately 25–30 GW per year [43].

## 2.4. Mapping energy resources to marginal and contaminated sites

Minimum site areas may restrict the number of sites on which renewable energy projects can be implemented. Table 3 lists suggested minimum site areas for each renewable energy option and compares the minimum areas with number and size of sites currently available. Different sizes of solar and wind technologies are given in the table to demonstrate the ranges available. Taking the example of algae biodiesel in Table 3, the photobioreactors require at least one acre of land [45,46], of which there are approximately 21,000 sites, totaling 1.72 million ha of land. This area analysis is separate from the climatic analysis, which would suggest in this example to site algae facilities in areas of high solar

insolation. Each additional analysis reduces the amount of land available for energy development.

Many permutations are possible to match the marginal and contaminated sites to respective energy crops and technologies. As previously mentioned, algae PBRs and solar PV systems should be sited in areas with high solar insolation, typically in the Southwest United States. Wind technologies should be sited in areas with the greatest wind resources, e.g. in the central region of the United States. Soybean and sunflower crops can be cultivated on sites with the least contamination and not better suited for solar and wind technologies. Soybean and sunflower crops also have the advantage of fitting small urban sites, whereas solar, wind, and algae technologies generally require larger pieces of land. Utility-scale technologies also require more land than decentralized or small-scale technologies. The calculations in this study focus on utility-scale development projects, while noting that the most comprehensive and sustainable energy solutions are likely to contain a mix of decentralized, mid-scale, and utility-scale projects.

Table 4 lists the total site areas nationally with the respective sunflower and soybean biodiesel production potentials. Biodiesel volumes were calculated based on a range of USDA census data and marginal values from the literature [31,33,34,47,48]. Given a soybean biodiesel energy content of 35.9 MJ/L and a sunflower biodiesel energy content of 33.7 MJ/L, marginal and contaminated sites including landfills, brownfields, and AMLs could produce between 5.22  10[3] TJ and 10.4  10[3] TJ of sunflower biodiesel (40.9–

78.6 MGY) or between 10.0  10[3] TJ and 13.3  10[3] TJ of soybean biodiesel (76.8–97.9 MGY). If half the sites were used for soybean biodiesel and the other half for sunflower biodiesel, the U.S. could produce 7.6  10[3] TJ–11.8  10[3] TJ per year (61.4–85.8 MGY).

Fig. 2 illustrates the microalgal growth rates at each site according to solar insolation. The PBRs used to grow the algae are typically located in regions with plentiful solar insolation, such as in the Southwestern United States. Using microalgal growth rates greater than or equal to 16 g/m[2] day as a lower-efficiency bound, and utilizing sites of at least one acre in size to accommodate the PBRs, the United States could produce 2.25  10[6] t of microalgal

biomass per year on marginal lands. Given an energy content of 41 MJ/kg and lipid content of 30%, 2.25  10[6] t is equivalent to 53.2  10[3] TJ per year or 1.50  10[9] L (396 MGY) of microalgal biodiesel [49]. Using microalgal growth rates greater than or equal to 18 g/m[2] day as a realistic upper efficiency bound, the U.S. could produce 821  10[3] t of microalgal biomass per year. This is equivalent to 33.6  10[3] TJ or 950  10[6] L (251 MGY) of microalgal biodiesel. Considering economic, technical, and logistical feasibility, growth rates closer to 18 g/m[2] day are more likely to be implemented as they provide the greater return on investment.

For the case of solar power, this study assumes a utility-scale single-axis tracking PV system (0° tilt) with a standard efficiency range of 0.15–0.35 [50–52]. Given these specifications, the U.S. – could produce 96.7 225 TW h/y of solar-based electricity. Total PV power production in a given geographic location is proportional to the size of the panel and the panel's peak output, both of which can vary considerably. Larger sites, or sites closer to densely populated areas, may benefit from larger networked systems.

When considering wind power, nearly half of the potential wind power sites examined in this study (46%) have a WPC that is considered marginal; 24% are ranked as “fair” and the remaining 30% have a ranking of “good” or better. To estimate the national wind power potential, the areas of brownfields, closed landfills, and AMLs were multiplied by the WPC ratings and a typical capacity factor range of 0.25–0.40 [41,42]. The U.S. could produce 18.1 TW h/y of wind-based electricity, using a 0.25 capacity factor on sites with fair to superb wind power ratings, to 27.5 TW h/y using a 0.40 capacity factor on sites with marginal to superb wind power ratings.

Table 5 summarizes the total potential biodiesel and electricity production if each energy source were produced on all mapped brownfields, closed landfills, and AMLs. Not all energy production methods will be used on all site types. Multi-criteria decision or optimization methods can be used to aid in energy site identification [53].

in the Eastern United States, will likely contribute to first- or secondgeneration liquid biofuels while the more heavily contaminated sites may be used for microalgal biofuels or solar- or wind-based electricity generation, where contamination levels and soil quality are less important. Solar and wind climatic conditions must also be favorable to implement non-agricultural technologies. In areas with both high solar insolation and less severe contamination, there is a trade-off between algae and solar production, and likewise between sunflower and soybean production. Some technology pairings are possible, e.g. wind farms and biofuel crops might be co-located on the same piece of land when cultivation and production conditions allow.

Conversion efficiencies affect the final production volumes. Biofuel conversion efficiencies vary widely depending on the feedstock and conversion pathway [54]. The agricultural feedstocks examined in this study have comparable conversion efficiencies. Sunflower oil has an average conversion efficiency of 93% [55] while soybean oil conversion efficiencies range from 90% to 98% [55]. Soybean and sunflower could be exchanged for more resilient crops, such as miscanthus or switchgrass, to maximize yields on contaminated soils. Microalgae conversion efficiencies can exceed 96% [56]. Depending on the specific technology employed, PV conversion efficiencies can range from 0.50 for residential systems to 0.95 for commercial systems [38]. Wind power conversion efficiencies can likewise reach 0.95 [57].

Renewable energy produced on contaminated sites can help satisfy the overall U.S. energy demand. In 2012, the U.S. consumed 1.20  10[5] TJ of biodiesel and 1.02  10[7] TJ of electricity (28.4  10[6] GW h) [58,59]. In comparison, the U.S. produced 64% of its combined biodiesel and electricity consumption in the same year from fossil fuels used to generate electricity alone. Given the five feedstocks and natural resources examined in this study, energy produced on contaminated sites could contribute up to 39% to the combined U.S. energy demand for biodiesel and electricity. The 39% estimate assumes wind turbines are installed on sites with a minimum 50-m wind density of 400 W/m[2] while solar installations and microalgal PBRs each occupy half of the sites with PV potential greater than 7.0 GW h/m[2] day, corresponding to microalgal biomass growth rates greater than 18.0 g/m[2] day. The remaining land is split equally between sunflower and soybean feedstocks. Fully realizing the 39% is unlikely, as it would be based on all technologies operating at optimal efficiency rates and at constant maximum capacity. Transportation logistics, technology implementation, and connection to the grid all need to be considered. These factors will reduce the total amount of energy available to the end user.

Not all contaminated land can or should be used for renewable energy development [60,61], nor should sites be completely abandoned following biofuel feedstock cultivation as this could lead to permanent land degradation [62]. Other uses can be sustainable and beneficial to the surrounding community. Such uses include urban food gardens [61,63,64], converted recreation areas [65], and commercial centers. The surrounding community should be consulted for development ideas to ensure the success and sustainability of the land reuse projects.

This study used brownfields, landfills, and abandoned mine lands to represent a subset of U.S. marginal lands. A broader marginal land analysis should ask what marginal land use scenarios represent the optimal use(s) of the respective lands and also produce the maximum volumes of desired types of renewable energy. Current land cover databases are limited in terms of soil quality recorded and spatial resolution of the data. In addition to lack of spatial data, there is also a lack of knowledge regarding feasible yields of energy crops on different types of marginal soils. Feedstocks such as camelina, switchgrass, and other perennial grasses could grow well in low-quality soils.

Availability of water needs to be considered for sunflower, soybean, and algae cultivation. While it can be expected that many sites in this study have some access to water given the nature of

their former uses as industrial sites, actual access will vary based on geographic location and project specifications. Algae-producing facilities can collaborate with wastewater treatment plants to reuse treated wastewater, which also provides necessary nutrients for algae growth [56,66]. Some irrigation is possible for sunflower and soybean sites, however the environmental and economic benefits of growing crops on these sites should exceed the respective costs of any irrigation for the projects to be sustainable. Out of the five renewable energy crops and technologies presented here, projects involving sunflower and soybean biodiesel crops will likely be most sensitive to water availability since water deficiency directly impacts oilseed production [67]. Further research is needed to better understand the efficiency and sustainability of on-site irrigation practices [68]. By optimizing the site type, energy source characteristics, and regional needs, marginal lands and contaminated sites can play an increasingly important role in meeting United States energy demands.

This study constructed and implemented a GIS model to evaluate a range of site-specific energy production potentials on brownfields, closed landfills, and abandoned mine lands. Five energy sources were considered: soybeans, sunflowers, and microalgae for biodiesel, and solar and wind for electricity. When all five resources on all three site types are allocated for optimal performance, energy produced on contaminated lands could help satisfy up to 39% of the total U.S. demand for diesel and electricity. Not all available land should be used for energy production; alternative uses include, for example, community-initiated food gardens and recreation areas.
